Hincmar of Reims
hĭngk´mär ŏv rēmz
n. (Hincmar, c. 806–882, archbishop of Reims, the most powerful churchman of the Carolingian West, who had Gottschalk flogged and imprisoned and opposed his doctrine of twofold predestination)
Germanic personal name. Archbishop of Reims from 845; a formidable canonist and administrator.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Hincmar was archbishop of Reims for nearly forty years and the leading prelate of the Frankish church. When Gottschalk taught twofold predestination, Hincmar had him condemned at the Synod of Quierzy in 849, flogged until he cast his writings into the fire, and confined at the monastery of Hautvillers for the rest of his life. At a second synod at Quierzy in 853 Hincmar issued four chapters: one predestination only, of the elect to life; God wills all men to be saved; Christ suffered for all; the free will lost in Adam is restored by grace. He pressed Paul's word that God “will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth” (1Ti 2:4), but passed over the Shepherd's own definition of His death: “I lay down my life for the sheep” (Joh 10:15), and His high-priestly prayer, “I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me” (Joh 17:9). Prudentius of Troyes, Ratramnus and the Council of Valence (855) opposed his chapters. His treatment of Gottschalk, who died refusing to recant, fell under James's sentence: “he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy” (Jas 2:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines prelate as an ecclesiastic of a higher order, as an archbishop, bishop or patriarch; a dignitary of the church.

PRELATE, n. An ecclesiastic of a higher order, as an archbishop, bishop or patriarch; a dignitary of the church.

Key Scripture

1Ti 2:4 — "Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth."

Joh 10:15 — "As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep."

Joh 17:9 — "I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine."

Jas 2:13 — "For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment."

Modern Corruption

Hincmar defended a universal redemption and a single predestination by flogging the monk who disagreed, and his doctrine is now the evangelical default while his methods are forgotten.

expand to see more

The chapters of Quierzy read like a modern statement of moderate evangelical soteriology: God wills all to be saved, Christ died for all equally, election is to life only, and no one is predestined to perdition. They were imposed by the most powerful archbishop in Europe on a monk who appealed to Augustine and Scripture. The contrast between the moderation of the doctrine and the brutality of its enforcement is a lesson of its own.

The 1689 Confession confesses particular redemption: to all those for whom Christ hath obtained eternal redemption, He doth certainly and effectually apply and communicate the same. Christ's intercession is for those given Him, and His death for His sheep. The recovery is that doctrine, held with the mercy Hincmar did not show.

Usage

"“Who will have all men to be saved” (1Ti 2:4) — Hincmar's proof text at Quierzy."

"“I lay down my life for the sheep” (Joh 10:15) — the Shepherd's own definition."

"“judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy” (Jas 2:13) — Hautvillers."
